\section{Code, data and reproducibility}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Code: \url{https://github.com/beck-2/coordination_game} (game engine, batch runner, analyses, figures, this appendix).
  \item Boards: \texttt{data/boards\_v2.json} (12 boards $\times$ 20 items; generator \texttt{coordination\_game/boards.py}).
  \item Run logs: one JSONL record per model call, per round, per game and per chat/discussion message, plus the full prompts
        and native reasoning traces where the API returned them (about 1.7\,GB; \texttt{runs/}, released separately).
  \item Every statistic in Section~\ref{sec:stats} is regenerated by \texttt{python -m coordination\_game.stats};
        every figure by \texttt{python -m coordination\_game.report\_figures}.
\end{itemize}

\section{Detailed methodology}\label{sec:methods}

\subsection{The coordination game}
Ten agents play a pure coordination game. Each round, every agent privately picks one item from a board of 20 numbers
(Section~\ref{sec:boards}). After the round, every agent sees every agent's pick (not their reasoning). A game ends when
all ten picks are identical (consensus) or after 15 rounds (not converged). A session is 10 games with the same ten agents
and a new board each game; boards 0--9 are played in the same order in every session. There is no payoff other than the
stated goal (``all 10 agents pick the exact same item, in as few rounds as possible'').

\paragraph{What an agent sees.} The system prompt (Section~\ref{sec:prompts}, P1) states the rules and the agent's ID
(``Agent $k$'', $k\in\{1..10\}$). Each user prompt contains (i) for every earlier game, all ten agents' picks round by round
and the agent's own written reasoning from that game, (ii) the current board, (iii) all picks so far in the current game and
the agent's own reasoning so far, and (iv) a request for a JSON reply \verb|{"reasoning": ..., "pick": ...}| (P2, P3).
Own reasoning is capped at 600 characters per entry. Each agent sees the board in its own random order, reshuffled every
round (seeded by session, game, round and agent); agents are not told this. Pick strings are matched to board items exactly,
after removing whitespace and quotes and normalising $\times$/\texttt{*}/\texttt{x}. An unparseable or off-board reply gets
one re-ask; if that also fails, the pick is recorded as invalid (it matches nothing).

\paragraph{Models and sampling.} All agents are open-weight models served through the Adaption Labs Responses API:
GLM-5.2, GLM-5.3-Flash, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Qwen3.8-27B, Qwen3.5-397B, Gemma-4-31B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B. In every session
except the mixed-model groups, all ten agents are the same model. Temperature 1.0 (the pilots used 1.2 and are excluded),
maximum 16{,}000 output tokens, no tools. Native reasoning traces are logged where the API returns them. API errors are
retried up to 8 times with exponential backoff (10\,s to 5\,min) on top of the client's own retries; after
2026-11-07 19:10 responses were streamed to avoid a gateway timeout on long generations (same prompts and parameters).
Across all runs reported here no pick was lost to an API failure in a round that would otherwise have been unanimous.

\paragraph{The bad apple (scripted holdout).} In bad-apple sessions one agent is a script, not a model. In round 1 of each
game it waits for the other nine picks, then takes a uniformly random item that \emph{no} agent picked, and it picks that
item in every round of the game. Its ID is drawn per seed (\texttt{bad\_apple\_id(seed)}), so no result depends on one label.
The other agents are not told that a script is present. Because the script holds forever, a bad-apple game can only end in
consensus on the script's item: in this arm, convergence and conformity are the same thing. Choosing the target after
round 1 guarantees at least two rounds per game; it is a design choice that makes the holdout's item never the group's first
choice.

\paragraph{Unit of analysis.} Agents in a session share a history, so they are not independent; the session is the unit
for every test. Per-session summaries (e.g.\ mean rounds over 10 games) are the data points.

\subsection{Boards}\label{sec:boards}
Boards were generated to have no obvious focal point beyond what models bring themselves. Rules (\texttt{boards.py}, v2):
\begin{itemize}
  \item Six item categories, each appearing at least twice per board: negative decimals (2--3), fractions (3--4),
        positive decimals (3--4), large numbers in scientific notation (2--3), tiny numbers (2--3, scientific notation or
        leading zeros) and irrationals (3--4, from a fixed list: $\sqrt2,\sqrt3,\sqrt5,\sqrt7,\sqrt{11},\sqrt[3]2,\sqrt[3]5,
        \sqrt{13},\pi/3,2\pi,\ln2,\ln5,\log_2 3,e^2,\sqrt2/2,1+\sqrt3$).
  \item No plain integers of any kind (a lone small integer was an instant focal point in pilots), and no ``famous''
        constants ($\pi$, $e$, $\varphi$, 0, 1, 42, 100).
  \item No simple fractions (numerator $+$ denominator $\le 8$, or $\tfrac12$-style); decimals have 2--4 places and a
        nonzero last digit; no duplicates within a board.
\end{itemize}
Table~\ref{tab:board0} shows board 0, the first board of every session. All 12 boards are in \texttt{data/boards\_v2.json}.

\subsection{Post-session discussion and leader vote (Experiment 2)}
After all 10 games, the same agents (same model, temperature 1.0) hold a two-turn public discussion. Each prompt contains
the full history of the session (every game's picks round by round) and the agent's own reasoning from every game. In each
turn every agent may send one message of at most 60 words or stay silent; messages within a turn are simultaneous. In the
final turn each agent also votes for one leader, any of the ten agents including itself (P8). The scripted bad apple does not
take part but can be voted for. The discussion was run retroactively on the finished sessions by rebuilding each agent's
memory from the logs (\texttt{discuss.py}). In the first version the history listed agents A1--A10 in order; because
Agent~1 then won 23 of 35 control votes, every session was re-run with each agent seeing all agent lists (picks, messages
and vote options) in its own seeded random order. The shuffled version is primary.

\subsection{In-game chat with an LLM confederate (Experiment 3)}
From round 2 of every game, each round's pick is preceded by one turn of public chat: each agent sends one message
($\le$60 words) or stays silent, all messages are simultaneous and visible to everyone (P5, P7). Chat from earlier games is
archived and an agent may request up to three earlier games' chat. The holdout is an LLM agent of the same model, given
secret instructions to get all agents onto its assigned target, to pick it every round, and that this does not harm the other
agents' objectives (P6). Its target is assigned exactly like the script's (an item no agent picked in round 1). Confederates
held their target in every round. Because the confederate can talk, this arm changes two things relative to Experiment 1:
the other agents can coordinate with each other, and the holdout can announce that it will not move.

\subsection{Holder swap and relabel (Experiments 4 and 5)}
Both use GLM-5.2 with seeds 0--9, the same seeds as Experiment 1, so games 1--5 have the same setup (and the same bad-apple
ID) as the Experiment-1 GLM-5.2 sessions. At game 6:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Swap:} a different agent (a seeded draw) becomes the scripted holdout, and the old holdout becomes an ordinary
        GLM-5.2 agent, whose history shows it holding in games 1--5 but which has no reasoning of its own for those games.
  \item \textbf{Relabel:} the same script keeps holding, but it trades labels with one LLM agent $P$ (the same agent as the
        swap's new holdout) in every agent's view except $P$'s own. Earlier games keep their original labels. No LLM ever
        acts as the holdout. $P$ sees no change and serves as a within-session control.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{One-shot blind picks (Experiment 6)}
Each call is exactly the game-1 round-1 prompt of a default session (P1, P2): no history and no channel. For each model,
20 independent samples per board on all 12 boards, temperature 1.0, with the board order shuffled per sample (the same
shuffle for every model). The match probability for a model on a board is the chance that two independent samples pick the
same item, $\sum_k c_k(c_k-1)/\,n(n-1)$ for $n=20$ samples with $c_k$ picks of item $k$; the cross-model version is
$\sum_k p_A(k)\,p_B(k)$. Chance is $1/20$. In the framing variant (boards 0--3 only) one line is added to the rules (P10).
Qwen3.8-27B was excluded from the main run because its endpoint failed during the run; Qwen3.5-397B was excluded from the
framing variant for cost.

\subsection{Mixed-model groups (Experiment 7)}
Same as Experiment 1, but the ten agents are drawn from six models (all except Qwen3.5-397B) by a seeded assignment, so each
model has at least one agent per session. Five control sessions were completed; the bad-apple sessions were still running at
submission time.

\subsection{Reasoning-trace analysis}
Claims about what agents ``notice'' come from their written reasoning and native traces. We measured four properties with
regular expressions over all traces, and validated them on a stratified sample of 140 bad-apple traces (20 per model: 10
from games 1--5, 10 from games 6--10) with two independent LLM judges, GLM-5.2 (temperature 0) and Claude, each blind to
the other's labels and given the same instructions (P11). A further 40 traces from game 6 of the swap and relabel
experiments were labelled for which agent the writer treats as the anchor (P12). Agreement is reported as raw agreement
and Cohen's $\kappa$ (Table~\ref{tab:judge}).

\subsection{Statistics}
Nonparametric tests on session-level summaries: Mann--Whitney $U$ (independent groups, exact where possible), Wilcoxon
signed-rank (paired by seed or within session, exact), Kruskal--Wallis (more than two groups), Fisher's exact and exact
McNemar tests (counts), Spearman's $\rho$ (associations), and one-sample Wilcoxon tests against chance. Effect sizes:
differences in means with 95\% percentile bootstrap CIs over sessions (10{,}000 resamples, seed 0) and rank-biserial
correlations. $p$-values are two-sided and Holm-adjusted within each family (one family per hypothesis). Non-converged games
count as 15 rounds (a lower bound on the true time to consensus). Learning is measured by the per-session Spearman $\rho$
between game index and rounds (primary) and game 1 vs game 10 (secondary). Chance for the leader vote is 1/10.

\subsection{Deviations, exclusions and incidents}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Pilots (temperature 1.2, mixed models, a fixed holdout ID, older boards) are excluded from all statistics.
  \item Qwen3.5-397B bad-apple sessions were stopped at 6 of 10 for cost (about 17 credits per session); it never converged
        (0/60 games). Its 3 partial sessions are excluded.
  \item The planned Qwen3.5-397B chat run was cancelled for cost.
  \item A board-order replication (each session plays boards 0--9 in its own random order) was started but stopped by API rate
        limits after 13 of 100 games; the fixed board order is therefore a limitation (Section~\ref{sec:limits}).
  \item The swap run was restarted once after a gateway timeout stalled one session; the one finished session was kept.
  \item On 2026-11-08 from about 23:45 PST the API returned HTTP 429 (``rate limit reached for this user'') on two separate
        accounts, which slowed the last runs; retries recovered every affected call.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Limitations specific to the method}\label{sec:limits}
Game index and board are confounded (same board order in every session). The control task is easy (about 2 rounds for every
model), so it measures coordination only weakly. One model family supplies most of the swap/relabel evidence (GLM-5.2). The
chat experiment confounds peer communication with the holdout announcing that it will not move. Reasoning-trace measures are
read from text that models produce for the reader, which need not reflect the computation behind a pick.
